title: Origin of complex multicellular life
summary: The oldest fossil showing complex multicellularity is the red alga Bangiomorpha, dated to about 1 billion years ago in one review and about 1.2 billion in another study. Multicellular organisms grow through cell differentiation and remodelling to produce an adult form. This fossil gives a minimum age for complex multicellular life, not the moment it began.

uncertainty.note: Dated by the earliest taxonomically resolved complex multicellular eukaryote, the red alga Bangiomorpha pubescens (~1.05 Ga to 1.2 Ga).

as_recorded.value: The oldest multicellular fossil exhibiting complex multicellularity, Bangiomorpha, is dated to ∼1 Ga

where.modern_name: No single place; stand-in pin at Somerset Island, Nunavut, Canada
where.historical_name: Not applicable (marine tidal shelf on supercontinent Rodinia; no modern political or geographic entities existed)

paleo.not_applicable: Deep time global biological transition in Mesoproterozoic to Neoproterozoic oceans across assembling supercontinent Rodinia.

importance.justification: The transition to multicellularity enabled cellular differentiation, macroscopic body plans, and specialized organs, founding all complex plant, animal, and fungal life.

related.because: Eukaryogenesis provided the endomembrane systems, nucleus, and bioenergetics required for the development of complex multicellularity.
Multicellularity and cellular differentiation were the evolutionary prerequisite for macroscopic metazoan body plans and animal diversification.
